entities.summary:
Gentius, the last attested king of the Illyrian Labeatan dynasty, reigned from 181 to 168 BCE, marking a pivotal, albeit tragic, chapter in the history of Illyria and its interactions with the burgeoning Roman Republic. His rule centered on Scodra (modern Shkodër, Albania), serving as the capital of an Illyrian kingdom increasingly caught between the geopolitical ambitions of Rome and the Macedonian Antigonid dynasty. Gentius inherited a complex diplomatic legacy from his father, Pleuratus III, who had maintained largely positive, if subordinate, relations with Rome, but the younger king's reign would ultimately culminate in the definitive loss of Illyrian independence.

The core of Gentius's reign was characterized by a delicate, and ultimately failed, balancing act amidst the great powers of the Hellenistic world. Initially maintaining a pro-Roman stance, his allegiances shifted dramatically by 169 BCE, when he forged an alliance with Perseus of Macedon, Rome's primary adversary in the Third Macedonian War. This strategic pivot was driven by a combination of perceived Roman encroachment, economic incentives, and perhaps a desperate bid to assert Illyrian sovereignty. Gentius's actions included impounding Roman ships and envoys, persecuting Roman allies among the Illyrians, and launching an attack on the cities of Apollonia and Dyrrachium, which were allied with Rome. This open defiance provoked Rome to declare the Third Illyrian War against him in 168 BCE.
